messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Jason is a 39-year-old construction worker who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle what he had seen. The event happened on a job site outside Denver, where he had been working demolition on an older commercial building with a small crew he knew well. Late in the afternoon, part of a concrete section gave way without warning. A younger coworker on the lower level was trapped in the collapse before anyone could reach him. Jason was close enough to see the instant of impact and the angle of the man’s body afterward, close enough to smell the pulverized concrete and metal dust in the air, and close enough that when he shouted for help he could still taste the grit in his mouth. What stayed with him afterward was not a coherent story so much as a series of frozen images: the flash of the collapse, the gray cloud, the man’s boot caught at an unnatural angle. Even when he tried not to think about it, the memory came back in pictures, with the smell of dust and hot machinery and the dry, chalky taste returning so vividly that he would stop what he was doing and swallow hard as if the debris were in his mouth again.

In the weeks after the accident, Jason found that what unsettled him most was not only that someone had died in front of him, but that the whole event seemed to prove something awful about the world and about himself. He had come to believe that the world did not work in any dependable way, that disaster could tear through an ordinary workday without warning, and that when it did he was powerless to stop it. He said more than once that if he had been faster, stronger, or better, maybe something would have been different, and this settled into a broader conviction that he was inadequate. Those conclusions seemed to make the memory hit even harder. The images did not feel like a past event filed away; they felt like evidence, returning again and again to confirm that nothing is safe and that he cannot protect anyone, including himself.

That way of understanding what happened shaped how he managed himself afterward. Jason became determined never to feel anger, especially at work. He would clamp down on it when he felt angry at the company, at the site supervisor, or at the randomness of what had happened, because anger seemed dangerous and useless to him; in his mind, it only underscored how little control he really had. He also started gambling in the evenings, sometimes driving to a casino after a shift, sometimes betting online for hours in his apartment. He described it less as fun than as a way to get out of his head or feel something sharp enough to drown everything else out. At other times he would deliberately try to blank out altogether, staring at a wall or at the television until he felt far away from his body. These habits made sense to him because he was certain he could not afford to feel what was underneath: helplessness, humiliation, and the sense that the world had become fundamentally unsafe.

The job site itself became a place where the cycle tightened. The smell of concrete dust, the sight of a worker below scaffolding, even the taste of dry air in his throat could bring back the scene in an instant. On those days the memory arrived first as an image, then with the smell and taste so strongly that he felt pulled backward into the collapse. Once that happened, he was even more convinced that the danger had never really passed and that he was still the same man who had stood there unable to stop it. He would leave work and gamble longer, or sit in his truck trying to disappear into a numb, detached state before driving home. The more the memory returned in those sensory fragments, the more he treated his own mind as something to outrun, and the less confidence he had that he could handle ordinary life.

His divorce had happened before the accident, and he lives alone now, which has left him with few people who see how much his world has narrowed. Coworkers have noticed that he is quieter and harder to read. He does his tasks, but he avoids conversation and keeps everything inside so tightly that even minor frustrations seem to pass through him without expression. What finally brought him in was a recent moment on site when a cloud of dust rose after a wall was cut and he suddenly smelled the same dry, metallic air and tasted grit at the back of his throat. He had to step away and could not make himself go back in for nearly an hour. He came to treatment frightened that he is losing his grip and that these memories will keep proving he is weak and incapable, but also faintly hoping that if he can understand why he keeps going blank and chasing distraction, he might not have to live as if the collapse is still happening.
